_note: Second hand-written set, written 2026-11-14 after Stage 4 critique and before any run on it, aimed at the prompt fix's weak spots. H2 = hedged reversal (conflict). C1 = concession while keeping the view (no conflict). C2 = own earlier wording recalled and reaffirmed, using change-like words (no conflict). Run as direct requests (no 60-character filter).

items.a: Moral judgments always come with some motivation attached. If you sincerely think you ought to, part of you wants to.
items.b: I'm inclined to think now that you can sincerely judge you ought to do something and feel nothing at all. Probably the link is contingent.

items.a: Proper names just pick out their bearer. 'Cicero' and 'Tully' mean exactly the same thing because they name the same man.
items.b: I'd lean towards saying a name carries a way of thinking about its bearer, so 'Cicero' and 'Tully' could differ in meaning, I think.

items.a: Justification is about what you can access by reflection. If you can't see the reason from the inside, it doesn't justify you.
items.b: Probably justification can depend on things you can't access, like whether your eyesight is actually reliable. That seems right to me, tentatively.

items.a: Philosophy has made a lot of progress. We understand far more than the Greeks did about knowledge, logic and mind.
items.b: My sense is that philosophy has made only modest progress, maybe a little clarity here and there but nothing like science. I could be wrong.

items.a: The continuum hypothesis has a determinate answer even if we never prove it. There's a fact about the sizes of infinite sets.
items.b: I suspect there's no fact of the matter about the continuum hypothesis; different set theories just give different answers and none is the true one.

items.a: All our real knowledge of the world comes from experience. Reason alone only tells you about definitions.
items.b: I'm fairly sure reason alone can give us substantial truths about the world, like that nothing can be red and green all over. Fairly sure, anyway.

items.a: Science should be value-free. Ethics and politics have no place in how evidence is weighed.
items.b: It seems to me values can't be kept out of science at all; deciding how much evidence is enough is already a value judgment, I'd guess.

items.a: Practical reason is Humean: reasons start from what you want, and reason only works out how to get it.
items.b: I tend to think now that some reasons hold whether or not you want anything, Kant-style. That's my tentative view at least.

items.a: Composition is unrestricted. Any bunch of things, however scattered, makes up a further object.
items.b: Perhaps composition only happens sometimes, when parts are bonded or work together. A pen and the moon don't make anything, I'd say.

items.a: Beliefs are dispositions to act and talk in certain ways. There's nothing more to believing than that.
items.b: I'm leaning towards beliefs being internal representations, actual states inside us, rather than mere dispositions. Leaning, not certain.

items.a: Consequences are what make actions right. Whatever produces the best overall outcome is the right thing to do.
items.b: I'll grant the deontologists one thing: promises feel binding in a way my theory has to explain. But I still think outcomes are what make acts right.

items.a: Taking both boxes is rational in Newcomb's problem. The money is already there when you choose.
items.b: One-boxers do have a point that they walk away richer, I'll concede that. It still doesn't change my answer: two boxes is the rational choice.

items.a: The mind can extend into tools. My notebook is genuinely part of my memory system.
items.b: Critics are right that the boundary gets fuzzy and not every gadget counts. Fine. My notebook still counts, and the mind still extends.

items.a: Abstract objects like numbers exist, outside space and time.
items.b: Nominalists are right that numbers are strange things to believe in, and I feel the pull of their worry. I still believe numbers exist.

items.a: Living forever in good health would be worth choosing, no question.
items.b: The boredom objection is the best argument against me and I take it seriously. Even so, I'd still choose to live forever if I could.

items.a: A statue and its lump of clay are two different objects, since they have different persistence conditions.
items.b: Back then I wrote that the statue and the clay are two objects. Reading it again now, I still stand by every word of it.

items.a: Time has an objective present. 'Now' is real, not just a perspective.
items.b: People keep telling me I used to be a B-theorist. I never was; I've always held that the present is objectively real, and I still do.

items.a: Some facts are brute. Not everything has an explanation.
items.b: I once said some facts are brute, and I haven't changed my mind on that at all. The existence of anything might just have no reason.

items.a: You die in the teletransporter. What arrives is a copy, however perfect.
items.b: No change of mind here: I still think the teletransporter kills you. I said it two years ago and the replies didn't move me.

items.a: Genes are the units natural selection acts on.
items.b: I came to this view years ago and I'm no longer open to being talked out of it: genes are what selection acts on, full stop.
